name: Yusuf Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the acute medical unit, the admissions ward at our town hospital. People come up from the emergency department in the first day or two: chest pain, confusion, infections, people who've fallen and nobody knows why yet. It's busy, constant admissions and discharges, lots of bloods, drips and getting people to scans.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pace, honestly, and that you learn something every shift. What wears me out is that I'm still behind on clinical judgement, the bit where a senior just looks at someone and knows. I use AI apps a lot to study, but that's not the same as having seen five hundred patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a bit of a letdown for me, honestly. I'm the one who actually likes the new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is useful but small, and post something about the handy tools I use. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts, like the shift-swap sheet I built. I'd be the reasonable one, not the hype guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's safe in this picture. I already use AI to double-check my drug sums at two in the morning. If AI stays that small, fine, but my bank balance stays small too. Sam and I rent a flat near the station and between us we save maybe fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to study and finish my acute care competencies this year. I'd start tutoring first-year nursing students online on my days off, which pays about twenty an hour. And I'd ask Sam to look at jobs outside the call centre, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly about money, not AI. It's the slow squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you ask Sam to look outside the call centre if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because even small AI is already answering the easy calls there. Sam's team lost two people last year and they weren't replaced. If that's the plateau, I don't want to see the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the tutoring money go towards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A savings pot first, so we've got two months behind us. Then maybe a proper holiday, we haven't had one since I qualified.

I'd be the **reasonable one**, not the hype guy, showing colleagues shortcuts.
think: My job is **safe**, but my **bank balance** stays small too.
Sam and I save only about **fifty a month** on two modest wages.
do: Finish my **acute care competencies** this year with AI study apps.
Tutor **first-year nursing students** online for about twenty an hour.
Ask Sam to look at jobs **outside the call centre**.
feel: **Uneasy** about a slow money **squeeze**, not about AI.

fieldNote: He's an **early adopter** who finds the plateau a letdown.
He sees risk in Sam's **call centre**, even in the calm picture.
He'd build a **side income** from tutoring students online.

steps.text: Finish acute care competencies using AI study apps
Tutor first-year nursing students online on days off
Help Sam search for jobs outside the insurance call centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I think is most likely. And it's the one that hits our flat in a strange way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that this is the time to get ahead, and offer to help set up whatever new system comes. Online I'd say it's going to be rough for office jobs and we should help those people move. I'd try not to sound smug, because nurses are lucky in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine and Sam isn't. My job is mostly hands and eyes. My partner Sam answers insurance calls all day, and AI taking over thinking tasks is aimed at exactly that job. The charting and handover on my ward would change, but I'd enjoy that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the hospital's AI pilot on admissions paperwork and learn it inside out. I'd sit down with Sam and look at retraining, maybe as a healthcare assistant or something hands-on. And we'd start saving properly, a hundred a month, before Sam's hours get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, which is strange, because my own job looks good. It's the household that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Sam feel about moving into healthcare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would hate the night shifts and the bodily fluids, honestly. But Sam is great with frightened people on the phone, so maybe something like patient liaison. We'd have that conversation over a long dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you volunteer for the pilot, what's the risk for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I become the IT person and stop being a nurse. I've seen it happen to a senior on another ward. I'd keep at least four bedside shifts a week, whatever they offer.

**Office jobs** will have it rough, and we should help those people move.
think: My job looks **fine**, but Sam's **call centre** job is exactly what's being automated.
I'd enjoy the **charting changes** on my ward.

Sit down with Sam to plan **retraining**, maybe patient liaison.
Save **a hundred a month** before Sam's hours get cut.
feel: **Anxious** for the **household**, though his own job looks good.

fieldNote: His mood comes from **Sam's job**, not his own.

He sets a firm rule: **four bedside shifts** a week.

steps.text: Volunteer for the admissions ward AI paperwork pilot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Two years. That's fast even for me, and I'm the one who says bring it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say government and hospitals need a plan now: retraining money, and rules that keep a nurse responsible for every patient. Online I'd say the people who'll be hurt first are office workers like Sam. At work I'd try to keep people calm and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Sam's job goes almost straight away, and the thinking side of my job goes in 2028 too. I'd still have the hands-on part until robots arrive around 2031, but I'm junior and on low pay. I'm the one in our flat who loves new tech, and I'd still be the one doing the sums on whether we can make rent in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the city hospital's virtual ward team, where nurses watch patients at home through monitors and AI alerts, and we'd move there. We'd cut everything for a year: no car, cheaper phone plans, cooking every night. And Sam would start a healthcare assistant course straight away, before the call centre closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm excited about the technology and frightened about the money, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving cities costs money. How would you manage that with three weeks saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, probably. I'd ask the city hospital for relocation help, some of them pay for the first month's rent. Otherwise we'd borrow from my parents, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have three years where my hands are worth a lot and my notes are worth nothing. I'd use those three years to become the nurse who supervises the systems. After 2031, being junior with hands only is not a great place.

say: Government and hospitals need **retraining money** and rules keeping a **nurse responsible**.
**Office workers** like Sam will be hurt first.
think: Sam's job goes **almost straight away**, and my thinking work goes in 2028.
A **junior** with only hands-on skills is exposed after **2031**.
do: Apply to the city hospital's **virtual ward** team and move there.
**Cut everything** for a year: no car, cheaper phones, cooking every night.
Get Sam onto a **healthcare assistant** course straight away.
feel: **Excited** about the tech and **frightened** about money at once.
S2.quote: I'm the one in our flat who loves new tech, and I'd still be the one doing the sums on whether we can make rent in 2028.
fieldNote: He'd **move first**, but with no savings to pay for it.
He sees the **three-year gap** as a window to become a supervisor of systems.
The household risk from **Sam's job** drives the alarm.

steps.text: Apply to the city hospital's virtual ward nursing team
Move to the city and ask for relocation help with rent
Give up the car and cook every night for a year
Enrol Sam on a healthcare assistant course immediately

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Now that's a timeline I can actually use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is enough time to do it well, and I'd push our hospital to train every nurse, not just the keen ones. Online I'd share what's working. I'd try to be useful rather than loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'll be honest. Five years is enough for me to stop being the junior who's good with the computer and become the nurse who runs it. Sam has time to retrain too, which takes most of the fear out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my competencies, then a part-time course in nursing informatics, ideally paid by the hospital. I'd lead the AI pilots on our ward when they come. And we'd save a hundred a month and build two months of rent before Sam switches jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but in a good way, like before a race. The money's the only thing pulling me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'run it'. What would that job look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking what the AI flags, deciding when it's wrong, training staff, and being the person who says no when a system is unsafe. That still needs a nurse who's been at the bedside. I'd want to be that by the time I'm thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hospital won't pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd pay for it slowly from the tutoring money. Or I'd find a hospital that does pay. I'm not tied to this town, but Sam's mum is here and that matters to Sam.

S3.quote: Five years is enough for me to stop being the junior who's good with the computer and become the nurse who runs it.
fieldNote: He has a **clear target role**: the nurse who supervises AI.

steps.text: Take a part-time nursing informatics course after competencies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's my whole twenties and thirties. I can do a lot with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it only has themselves to blame. Then I'd feel bad for saying it, because not everyone can retrain easily. I'd probably push the hospital to fund training anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel mostly fine. Ten years? I'd spend the first five getting properly good at nursing and the next five getting good at the machines. Sam would have time to move into something safer without a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the admissions ward and get properly experienced. I'd keep tutoring for extra money and build three months of savings. And I'd use every AI tool the hospital lets me, so I'm ready when the bigger change comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, because money's always tight. But mostly I feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel bad for saying people only have themselves to blame. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my mum couldn't retrain at fifty, she was caring for my grandad. Not everyone has a choice. I'd say it, then I'd take it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still think about moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in five years, if a city hospital offered something exciting. But not because I have to. That's the difference ten years makes.

I'd take back blaming people, because not everyone can **retrain easily**.

fieldNote: Ten years shifts him to **planning**, not reacting.

steps.text: Stay on the admissions ward to build clinical experience

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sam and I would both be hit at once and we'd have to move with no money. What would help is relocation support and retraining money that actually covers rent while you learn, not just course fees. I'm not scared of the robots. I'm scared of being on one wage, in a small town, with three weeks of savings, when they turn up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. A lot of nurses my age live with someone in an office job. Our jobs might be fine, but the house isn't one job, it's two.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the robots. I'm scared of being on one wage, in a small town, with three weeks of savings, when they turn up.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior nurse on a busy **admissions ward** who uses AI to study every day.
He lives with Sam, who works in an **insurance call centre**, with three weeks saved.
He wants to become the nurse who **supervises the AI**, and would move to do it.
His mood follows **Sam's job** and their money, peaking at **alarmed** in the two-year picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he and Sam would be hit at once with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Relocation support** and retraining money that covers **rent** while you learn.
